short: The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI was adopted in November 2021 by all 193 member states. It is the only AI ethics instrument with universal membership. It sets values, principles and eleven policy areas, and it is implemented through a Readiness Assessment Methodology and an Ethical Impact Assessment that countries and organizations can run.
title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
subtitle: The 2021 global standard adopted by all 193 UNESCO member states
body_html:
What the Recommendation is

The Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence was adopted by the UNESCO General Conference on November 23, 2021, by all 193 member states. It is a standard-setting instrument under UNESCO's constitution, which means member states report on implementation but are not legally bound. It is the broadest AI ethics agreement by membership; the OECD principles have 47 adherents, this one has every UN member that belongs to UNESCO.

What it covers

Four values: human rights and dignity; living in peaceful, just and interconnected societies; ensuring diversity and inclusiveness; and environment and ecosystem flourishing.

Ten principles: proportionality and do no harm, safety and security, fairness and non-discrimination, sustainability, right to privacy and data protection, human oversight and determination, transparency and explainability, responsibility and accountability, awareness and literacy, and multi-stakeholder governance.

Eleven policy areas where governments are asked to act, including ethical impact assessment, data policy, gender, education, labor, health, and environment.

How it is implemented

  • Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM). A country-level assessment of laws, institutions and capacity against the Recommendation. More than fifty countries have run or started one.
  • Ethical Impact Assessment (EIA). A project-level tool for a government or organization procuring or deploying an AI system, structured around the ten principles.
  • Global Forum on the Ethics of AI. An annual meeting where states report progress.

Why it matters

For countries without an AI law, the Recommendation is often the first national AI policy reference, and the RAM is the first assessment their government runs. For companies, the EIA is a free, published impact assessment template that predates ISO/IEC 42005 and covers many of the same questions.

What a claim does not mean

No state is bound and no organization is certified. A company that says it follows the UNESCO Recommendation has adopted its principles voluntarily; the claim can be checked only against what the company publishes.

Related instruments

The OECD AI Principles are the narrower, older counterpart. The Council of Europe Framework Convention is the binding treaty. The ISO/IEC 42005 impact assessment standard is the industry counterpart to the EIA. See the Standards and Frameworks hub.

Primary sources
